analysis.one_liner: Requires the SEC to track private equity ownership of childcare centers and blocks quick profits on newly bought ones.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in July 2026 and referred to two House committees, where no further action has been taken; no hearing, markup, or floor vote has occurred.
analysis.plain_summary: Private equity firms have been buying up chains of childcare centers in recent years, often restructuring them to pay for their purchase with dividends, fee income, or a quick resale. This bill would require large investment funds that control more than 25 childcare locations to report every purchase and sale of a childcare business to the Securities and Exchange Commission, with an annual report to Congress. It would also bar a fund from selling its stake in, or taking dividend payouts or buybacks out of, a newly acquired childcare company for four years. And it directs a government watchdog study of how private equity ownership affects care quality, available spots, tuition, and worker wages.
analysis.who_benefits: Parents who depend on childcare, children in these centers, and childcare workers. The reporting would give Congress and regulators, for the first time, a full picture of which funds own which centers. The four-year restriction on selling, dividends, and buybacks would make it harder for a fund to buy a chain, strip cash out of it, and flip it — the pattern most associated with rising tuition, cost cuts, and center closures.

how_it_helps.text: Requires large private funds controlling childcare at more than 25 locations to report their purchases, sales, and ownership of childcare businesses to the SEC, with an annual anonymized report to Congress [S2].

Bars a covered fund from selling any interest in a newly acquired childcare company, or taking a dividend payment, capital distribution, or share buyback from it, for four years after acquiring control [S2].

Directs the Government Accountability Office to study how private equity ownership affects quality of care, availability of spots, tuition, and employee wages, and report findings to Congress within two years [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Private equity funds and other investment funds with over $150 million under management that control large childcare chains. They would face new SEC reporting costs and a four-year freeze on cashing out of newly bought childcare companies. If those restrictions make childcare investments less profitable, some funds might buy fewer childcare companies — which could reduce the capital available to expand childcare supply, though the bill's supporters see the current investment as doing more harm than good.

drawbacks.text: The bill only covers funds with more than $150 million in assets under management controlling childcare at more than 25 locations, so many smaller operators and chains are untouched [S2].
It regulates through disclosure and a holding period rather than capping tuition or setting quality standards, so families could pay the same prices even if the bill became law [S2].

The four-year ban on sales and dividends could make childcare companies less attractive to investors of any kind, potentially reducing capital available to open new centers — a cost an honest supporter would acknowledge even while judging it worthwhile.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits run to families, children, and workers, and the costs fall mainly on a small set of large investment funds. The bill is a first step — more about shining light and stopping the fastest profit-taking than fixing prices or quality directly — and its narrow thresholds leave smaller chains uncovered. But the direct cost to ordinary people is small, and the GAO study could lay the groundwork for stronger rules later.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in late July 2026 and sent to the Financial Services and Education and Workforce committees, and neither committee has taken it up since.

narrative.text: Rep. Josh Riley of New York introduced the bill on July 22, 2026, with five Democratic cosponsors [S1] [S2] [S4].
It was referred to the Committee on Financial Services and, in addition, the Committee on Education and Workforce, pending the Speaker's decision on which committee handles which provisions [S4].
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor action has occurred since introduction; the bill remains pending with the Congress still in session [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private equity funds are better off for now: no disclosure requirement or profit restriction applies to them while the bill sits untouched in committee, and the current rules on buying and flipping childcare companies remain unchanged.

for.name: Rep. Josh Riley
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and lined up initial support

for.name: Reps. Greg Casar, Gilbert Cisneros, April McClain Delaney, Suhas Subramanyam, and Eugene Vindman
for.what_they_did: Signed on as original cosponsors at introduction

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all five cosponsors are Democrats; no House Republican has cosponsored, and no committee or floor vote has yet shown where the parties stand.

industries.industry: Private equity and large private funds
industries.note: Funds with over $150 million under management controlling childcare at more than 25 locations would have to report all childcare deals to the SEC and could not take dividends, buybacks, or a sale out of a newly bought childcare company for four years. The bill targets exactly the rapid profit-taking — cash-out dividends and quick flips — that has driven concerns about rising tuition and weaker care at private equity-owned chains.

Large childcare chains owned by covered funds would operate under the new restrictions, which could limit how their owners extract cash. Smaller and independent providers, below the 25-location and $150 million thresholds, are not covered at all.

analysis.trajectory: With five months left in the session, two committees sharing jurisdiction, and a handful of cosponsors, the bill would need a chair to schedule a hearing or markup and House leadership to schedule a vote — steps that have not begun. Bills referred to two committees with this little support most often die quietly at the end of the Congress.
